title: RPA Failure & Knowledge Copilot
tagline: An AI layer over a large bot estate that turns silent automation failures into diagnosed root causes, and unread process design documents into a conversational knowledge assistant for new developers.
role: AI Engineer — RAG architecture, document structure modelling, failure analysis design
headline: Two failures of a large automation programme — bots that break silently and documentation nobody reads — solved with one retrieval architecture.
highlights: Section-aware chunking that models a process document's real structure instead of splitting by sentence
Chunk-type metadata (process step, exception, scope) that makes retrieval filterable, not just semantic
Failure-log analysis that groups recurring bot errors into root causes rather than listing incidents
Fully local embeddings — process documents never leave the network
Answers grounded in the source document with the step or exception cited
context: Organisations running hundreds of automation bots across business units live with two chronic, expensive problems. Bots fail without a clear root cause, and developers spend hours reconstructing why from logs. Meanwhile the process design documents that explain what each bot does — the institutional knowledge of the whole programme — sit unread, so new developers repeat mistakes that were documented years earlier.
problem:
### Two problems, one underlying cause

Both failures come from the same place: **the knowledge exists but cannot be reached at the moment it is needed**.

**Failure reports are buried and repetitive.** Bot failures arrive as log entries and email notifications. Individually they are noise; in aggregate they contain a small number of recurring root causes. Nobody has time to do that aggregation by hand, so the same failure is diagnosed from scratch repeatedly.

**Process documents are structured in a way naive retrieval destroys.** A process design document is not prose. It contains an overview, a numbered process-step table, screenshot descriptions, an exception table and scope annexures — each with completely different retrieval characteristics. Splitting it by sentence produces chunks that cut a process step in half and mix an exception into an annexure, and the resulting answers are confidently wrong about the sequence of a process.

**The questions are specific.** "What transaction code is used?", "Walk me through the process", "What happens if the source system is unavailable?" These need exact steps and exact exception handling, not a topical summary.

**The content is sensitive.** Process documents describe internal systems and controls in detail, which rules out sending them to an external service.
approach:
The decision that carried the whole project was refusing to treat a process design document as unstructured text.

These documents have **distinct semantic zones**, and each one wants different handling. The overview is dense context needing low granularity. The process-step table is structured — each row is an atomic unit and must never be split. Screenshot descriptions are retrieval noise. The exception table is small and high-precision and should stay whole. So I chunk by section first, then split oversized sections by paragraph with overlap, and attach **metadata to every chunk**: which document, which section, which step number, which page, and critically what *type* of content it is.

That chunk-type field is what makes the difference. "What happens if the system is down?" filters to exception chunks before ranking. "Walk me through the process" retrieves process-step chunks in step order rather than in similarity order. Retrieval stops being a similarity search and becomes a structured query with a semantic component.

For failure analysis, the same instinct applied: the useful output is not a list of incidents but a grouping into recurring causes, so the system aggregates before it summarises.
solution:
Process design documents are parsed with layout awareness, using table-aware extraction for the process-step and exception tables where general text extraction loses row structure. Content is chunked by section, with oversized sections split by paragraph under overlap, and every chunk carries document, section, step number, page and chunk-type metadata.

Embeddings are generated by a locally-hosted encoder and stored in a local vector database, so no document content leaves the network. A question is answered by filtering on chunk type where the question implies one, retrieving semantically within that scope, and generating a grounded answer that cites the specific step or exception it came from.

In parallel, bot failure logs are parsed and grouped by error signature so recurring failures collapse into a small set of root causes with frequency and affected processes, rather than presenting as an undifferentiated incident stream.

systemDesign.overview: A retrieval system built around document structure rather than raw text. Ingestion preserves the semantic zones of a process document; the index stores structural metadata alongside vectors; the query layer uses that metadata to constrain retrieval before ranking.

components.name: Structure-aware parser
components.responsibility: Extracts text with page and layout information, using table-aware parsing for process-step and exception tables where row structure matters

components.name: Section-aware chunker
components.responsibility: Chunks by document section first, splits oversized sections by paragraph with overlap, and keeps table rows atomic

components.name: Metadata enricher
components.responsibility: Attaches document id, section name, step number, page and chunk type to every chunk so retrieval can filter structurally

components.name: Local embedding service
components.responsibility: Generates embeddings entirely on-premises so process documentation never leaves the network

components.name: Vector store
components.responsibility: Stores vectors with their structural metadata, supporting filtered semantic retrieval

components.name: Query router
components.responsibility: Detects question intent and constrains retrieval to the relevant chunk type before semantic ranking

components.name: Grounded answerer
components.responsibility: Generates structured answers citing the specific process step or exception the content came from

components.name: Failure aggregator
components.responsibility: Parses bot failure logs and groups them by error signature into recurring root causes with frequency and affected processes

dataFlow.detail: The process document is parsed with page and layout awareness, using table-aware extraction where row structure carries the meaning.
Content is divided into its semantic zones — overview, process steps, exceptions, scope — rather than split by length.
Each zone is chunked appropriately, with table rows kept atomic, and every chunk tagged with section, step number, page and chunk type.
A local encoder generates embeddings, which are persisted with their metadata in the local vector store.
An incoming question is inspected for intent — a process walkthrough, an exception question, a lookup — and retrieval is constrained to the matching chunk type.
Semantic retrieval runs within the filtered scope; process-step results are returned in step order rather than similarity order.
A grounded answer is generated, citing the step number or exception it came from so the reader can verify it against the source.

aiEngineering.summary: The interesting engineering here is not the model — it is the ingestion. This project is a demonstration that retrieval quality on structured documents is a data-modelling problem, and that chunking strategy determines the ceiling on answer quality far more than model choice does.

models.name: all-MiniLM-L6-v2 (local)
models.why: Loaded from local weights with no external call, which was a hard requirement because process documents describe internal systems and controls. Small enough to run alongside everything else, and entirely adequate for retrieval within a bounded document corpus where metadata filtering already does much of the narrowing.

models.name: Azure OpenAI — GPT-4.1 mini
models.why: Only retrieved chunks are ever sent for generation, never whole documents, so exposure is bounded to the passages needed to answer. The task is structured summarisation of retrieved steps, which a smaller model handles reliably and cheaply enough for interactive use.

aiEngineering.retrieval: Retrieval is filtered before it is semantic. Every chunk carries a type — process_step, exception, overview, scope — and the query router constrains the search space by intent before ranking within it. An exception question never competes against process-step chunks, and a walkthrough request returns steps ordered by step number rather than by cosine similarity. Screenshot descriptions are dropped at ingestion because they are pure retrieval noise. Process-step and exception table rows are kept atomic, since half a step is worse than no step.
aiEngineering.evaluation: Evaluation used the questions the system actually has to answer: transaction-code lookups, full process walkthroughs, and exception-path questions. The measures that mattered were whether a walkthrough returned every step in the correct order with none missing, and whether exception questions retrieved the right exception rather than a topically similar process step. Sentence-level chunking failed both consistently, which is what drove the structural approach — the comparison was the evidence, not an assumption.
aiEngineering.guardrails: Answers are generated only from retrieved chunks and cite the step number, exception or page they came from, so a reader can verify against the source document. When retrieval returns nothing within the filtered scope, the system says so rather than widening the search and answering from loosely related content — for a process document, a plausible but wrong step is more damaging than an admitted gap.

infrastructure.hosting: Runs on an Azure VM inside the corporate network, with local model weights and a locally-persisted vector store; only retrieved passages reach the tenant's Azure OpenAI deployment.
infrastructure.rationale: Process design documents describe internal systems, credentials handling and control steps in detail, so keeping ingestion, embedding and the vector store entirely on the VM meant no document ever crossed a network boundary in full. Running the encoder locally also removed per-document embedding cost, which mattered because the whole corpus is re-embedded whenever the chunking strategy changes — and during a two-week build, that happened repeatedly.
infrastructure.dataResidency: Documents, chunks and embeddings never leave the corporate network. Generation sends only the specific retrieved passages to the tenant-hosted model, never whole documents.

decisions.issue: How to chunk a process design document
decisions.choice: Section-aware chunking with typed metadata, keeping table rows atomic — not fixed-size or sentence splitting
decisions.rationale: These documents have distinct semantic zones with different retrieval characteristics. Naive splitting cuts process steps in half and blends exceptions into annexures, producing answers that are confidently wrong about sequence. Structure is the signal, and discarding it caps answer quality regardless of model.
decisions.tradeoff: Ingestion is coupled to document structure, so a materially different document template needs parser work rather than working automatically.

decisions.issue: Pure semantic retrieval or metadata-filtered retrieval
decisions.choice: Filter by chunk type on question intent, then rank semantically within scope
decisions.rationale: An exception question and a process step can be semantically similar while being completely different answers. Filtering first removes an entire class of plausible-but-wrong retrieval, and it makes step-ordered walkthroughs possible at all.
decisions.tradeoff: Requires intent detection, which can misroute. Mitigated by falling back to unfiltered retrieval rather than returning nothing when intent is ambiguous.

decisions.choice: Local encoder with local vector persistence
decisions.rationale: Process documents detail internal systems and controls. Beyond the compliance position, local embedding removed per-document cost during a period when the corpus was re-embedded repeatedly as the chunking strategy evolved.
decisions.tradeoff: A smaller encoder than a hosted frontier model — largely offset because metadata filtering already narrows the candidate set before semantics matter.

decisions.issue: Failure logs: list incidents or aggregate causes
decisions.choice: Group by error signature into recurring root causes with frequency and affected processes
decisions.rationale: An incident list is what the team already had and could not use. The value is in noticing that thirty failures across six bots share one cause — aggregation is the analysis, and summarising an unaggregated stream just produces a longer list.
decisions.tradeoff: Signature grouping can merge genuinely distinct failures that share an error surface, so groups carry examples for inspection rather than being treated as final.

challenges.title: Naive chunking made the assistant confidently wrong
challenges.description: The first ingestion used standard sentence-based splitting with overlap. Answers looked fluent and were unreliable in the worst way — process walkthroughs skipped steps or returned them out of order, and exception answers pulled text from unrelated sections. Fluent and wrong is harder to catch than obviously broken.
challenges.solution: I rebuilt ingestion around document structure: chunk by section, keep process-step and exception rows atomic, drop screenshot descriptions, and tag every chunk with its type and step number. Walkthroughs then returned complete, correctly ordered steps because ordering came from metadata rather than from similarity ranking.

challenges.title: Tables that general text extraction flattened
challenges.description: Process-step and exception tables carry the highest-value content, and general PDF text extraction flattens them into runs of text where step numbers, descriptions and manual/automated flags lose their column association.
challenges.solution: I used table-aware extraction specifically for those sections while keeping the faster general extractor for prose, so each part of the document is parsed by the tool that handles it best. Row structure survived into the chunks, which is what made step-level metadata possible at all.

challenges.title: Similar questions needing different retrieval scopes
challenges.description: "What does step 4 do?" and "What happens if step 4 fails?" are lexically and semantically close but must retrieve from different parts of the document. Pure similarity search returned the process step for both, so exception handling was routinely missed.
challenges.solution: The query router detects exception-shaped questions and constrains retrieval to exception chunks before ranking. Because exception tables are small and now retrieved in isolation, precision on that question class went from unreliable to dependable.

challenges.title: Failure noise that resisted summarisation
challenges.description: Summarising raw failure logs produced a longer restatement of the same noise. The logs contained the answer, but only in aggregate — no individual entry reveals that a recurring cause is responsible for a large share of downtime.
challenges.solution: I aggregated by error signature before any summarisation, so the output is a ranked set of root causes with frequency and affected processes, each carrying example incidents. The analysis step is the grouping; the model only writes up an already-computed result.

results.description: From problem framing to a working platform covering both failure analysis and document Q&A.
Step metadata replaced similarity ranking, so process walkthroughs stopped skipping or reordering steps.
Intent routing stopped exception queries returning topically similar process steps.
Ingestion and embedding stay on-network; only retrieved chunks reach the model.
Signature aggregation collapses a stream of failures into a ranked set of recurring root causes.
